title: Knowledge, Information Sources, Attitudes, and Personal Use of Complementary and Integrative Therapies Among Undergraduate Nursing Students: A Pre–Post Educational Intervention Evaluation
content: Background: Complementary and integrative therapies (CITs) are increasingly demanded, yet formal university training remains limited. This study evaluated overall knowledge, information sources, attitudes, and personal use of CITs among undergraduate nursing students before and after a dedicated course. Methods: A quasi-experimental study with two aggregated cross-sectional evaluations (pretest/posttest) was conducted in a second-year nursing cohort (N=135). An ad-hoc validated questionnaire was administered anonymously at baseline (n=106) and after completing an obligatory course on evidence-based complementary care (n=110). Results: Following the educational intervention, overall CIT knowledge expanded across the cohort. The university course became the predominant information source (87.3%), reducing reliance on social media (59.1%) and increasing consults of scientific literature (33.6%). Overall, 100 % of post-intervention respondents acknowledged the necessity of CIT knowledge for patient education. Support for mandatory curricular inclusion rose from 12.3% to 36.4%, while 56.4% favoured public healthcare integration conditional upon proven efficacy and safety. Conclusions: Course completion was associated with higher overall CIT knowledge, a shift toward evidence-based information sources, and favourable professional attitudes at the group level. Integrating evidence-based CIT education into nursing curricula is essential for fostering safe clinical practice.
